lmsArticle.title: Spark Structured Streaming: Micro-Batch vs Continuous Processing
lmsArticle.subtitle: Treats streams as unbounded tables — the execution model determines whether your pipeline hits milliseconds or minutes.

📖 The 15-Minute Gap: How a Fraud Team Discovered They Needed Real-Time Streaming
A fintech team runs payment fraud detection with a well-tuned Spark batch job. Every 15 minutes it reads a day's worth
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

<!--

A fintech team runs payment fraud detection with a well-tuned Spark batch job. Every 15 minutes it reads a day's worth of transaction events from S3, scores them against a model, and writes flagged payments to a PostgreSQL alerts table. It works. The false-positive rate is low, the job completes in under three minutes, and the pipeline has been stable for months.

Then the fraud team reviews a case where a sto…

This walkthrough focuses on **The 15-Minute Gap: How a Fraud Team Discovered They Needed Real-Time Streaming**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- A fintech team runs payment fraud detection with a well-tuned Spark batch job.
- Every 15 minutes it reads a day's worth of transaction events from S3, scores them against a model, and writes flagged payments to a PostgreSQL alerts table.
- The false-positive rate is low, the job completes in under three minutes, and the pipeline has been stable for months.

**Concepts in play:** spark-data-engineering, event-driven-architecture, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, data-warehousing-lakehouse

## Stage 1 — Streams as Unbounded Tables: The Core Abstraction of Structured Streaming

- Structured Streaming reframes how engineers think about data in motion.
- In the traditional batch model, a dataset is a finite, bounded table: you read it all, compute results, and write output.
- In Structured Streaming, a data stream is modelled as an unbounded table — a table that never stops growing because new rows are constantly being appended by the source (a Kafka topic, a file directory, a socket).
- Reading and Writing a Stream To consume a stream, you use readStream on a SparkSession .

*Applies **spark-data-engineering** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Reading and Writing a Stream To consume a stream, you use readStream on a SparkSession .

## Stage 2 — Inside MicroBatchExecution: How Every Trigger Fires a Batch Job

- The default and most commonly used execution engine in Structured Streaming is MicroBatchExecution .
- Understanding it moves you from "I follow the docs" to "I can debug production incidents." The StreamExecution Thread When you call writeStream.start() , Spark starts a dedicated StreamExecution thread for the query.
- This thread runs in a loop and is managed by StreamingQueryManager , a singleton component in the SparkSession that tracks all active streaming queries, enforces resource policies, and provides the awaitAnyTermination()…
- The loop proceeds in four phases for every trigger interval: 1.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Trigger fires"] --> B["Poll sources for new offsets"]
    B --> C["Write end offsets to offset WAL"]
    C --> D["Execute Spark batch job over offset range"]
    D --> E["Write committed epoch to commit WAL"]
    E --> F{"More data or trigger?"}
    F -- Yes --> B
    F -- No --> G["Query idle - waiting for next trigger"]
```

```
<checkpointDir>/
  offsets/        # WAL: planned end offsets per micro-batch epoch
  commits/        # WAL: committed epochs after successful batch
  state/          # State store data for stateful operators (windows, dedup, joins)
  metadata        # Query ID, Spark version, config snapshot
```

**Observable outcome:** The loop proceeds in four phases for every trigger interval: 1.

## Stage 3 — How Structured Streaming Guarantees Correctness at Scale

- The Internals of MicroBatchExecution MicroBatchExecution extends StreamExecution , which is the base class for all Spark streaming execution engines.
- The object hierarchy is worth knowing when reading stack traces or Spark source code: Epoch-based offset tracking is how Structured Streaming achieves determinism.
- Each micro-batch is assigned a monotonically increasing epoch number (the batch ID).
- The offset log and commit log are both indexed by this epoch number.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```
StreamingQueryManager  (1 per SparkSession)
  └── StreamingQuery   (1 per active stream)
        └── StreamExecution  (abstract)
              └── MicroBatchExecution  (default engine)
              └── ContinuousExecution  (experimental engine)
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Measure processingTime vs triggerInterval"] --> B{"processingTime > triggerInterval?"}
    B -- No --> C["Pipeline healthy - trigger interval is fine"]
    B -- Yes --> D{"inputRows > processedRows per second?"}
    D -- No --> E["Transient spike - monitor but no action"]
    D -- Yes --> F["Backlog is growing"]
    F --> G["Check maxOffsetsPerTrigger setting"]
    G --> H{"Resource bottleneck?"}
    H -- Yes --> I["Add executors or increase executor memory"]
    H -- No --> J["Reduce shuffle partitions or simplify stateful ops"]
```

**Observable outcome:** The offset log and commit log are both indexed by this epoch number.

## Stage 4 — The End-to-End Streaming Pipeline: From Kafka to Sink

- The following diagram shows how data flows through a Structured Streaming pipeline backed by Kafka and writing to Delta Lake.
- Each component maps to a concrete class or abstraction in Spark's codebase.
- The offset WAL (top-right loop) is written before the batch executes.
- The commit WAL (bottom loop) is written after the batch succeeds.

*Applies **data-warehousing-lakehouse** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Kafka Topic - Source] --> B[KafkaSource - offset polling]
    B --> C[MicroBatchExecution - trigger loop]
    C --> D[Offset WAL - offsets dir]
    D --> C
    C --> E[Spark Batch Job - Catalyst plan]
    E --> F[State Store - windows and dedup]
    F --> G[DataStreamWriter - writeStream]
    G --> H[Delta Lake Sink - transactional write]
    H --> I[Commit WAL - commits dir]
    I --> C
    C --> J[StreamingQueryManager - lifecycle]
    J --> C
```

**Observable outcome:** The commit WAL (bottom loop) is written after the batch succeeds.

## Stage 5 — Real-World Patterns: Kafka, Incremental File ETL, and Delta Lake Sinks

- Kafka Source with Structured Streaming Kafka is the most common source for Structured Streaming production deployments.
- The KafkaSource maps each Kafka partition to a Spark task and tracks {topic, partition, offset} triples as the offset state.
- The source guarantees that each offset range is processed exactly once across restarts.
- A critical operational detail: Spark does not commit offsets back to Kafka's consumer offsets topic by default.

*Applies **spark-data-engineering** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** A critical operational detail: Spark does not commit offsets back to Kafka's consumer offsets topic by default.

## Stage 6 — Choosing the Right Streaming Execution Mode for Your Pipeline

- Use this table to map your pipeline's constraints to the appropriate execution model.
- A few rules of thumb that will save a post-mortem: Do not choose Continuous processing for stateful work.
- It will either not compile or silently produce incorrect results for operators like groupBy , window , and dropDuplicates .
- Do not tune your way out of an undersized cluster.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Define latency requirement"] --> B{"Latency > 1 minute?"}
    B -- Yes --> C["AvailableNow trigger - batch-style incremental ETL"]
    B -- No --> D{"Latency 1s to 60s?"}
    D -- Yes --> E{"Complex stateful ops?"}
    E -- Yes --> F["Micro-Batch + RocksDB state store"]
    E -- No --> G["Micro-Batch default trigger"]
    D -- No --> H{"Sub-100ms with full state?"}
    H -- Yes --> I["Apache Flink"]
    H -- No --> J["Spark Continuous (experimental - stateless only)"]
```

**Observable outcome:** Do not tune your way out of an undersized cluster.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Lesson 1: The checkpoint is not optional — treat it like a database.
- Teams routinely point the checkpoint location at a local filesystem or ephemeral NFS mount for development convenience and then forget to change it before deploying to production.
- TLDR: Spark Structured Streaming models a data stream as an unbounded table and executes queries over it using the micro-batch engine ( MicroBatchExecution ).
- Each trigger fires a Spark batch job over a bounded offset range.

## Alternatives considered

### These three execution models represent genuinely different tradeoffs — not just a dial turned from slow to fast.

These three execution models represent genuinely different tradeoffs — not just a dial turned from slow to fast.

### Micro-Batch (Structured Streaming default)

The micro-batch engine achieves latency in the range of 100ms to several seconds depending on trigger configuration and cluster size.

### Continuous Processing (Spark experimental)

Continuous processing ( Trigger.Continuous("1 second") ) eliminates the micro-batch boundary.

### Apache Flink

Flink's streaming runtime is a true event-at-a-time engine.


## Failure and degraded modes

The source does not isolate a separate failure mode. Limits that matter for the scenario are called out in the stage decisions above.

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
